strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: leveraging known/learned decomposability of discrete objective functions for more sample-efficient distributional optimization (EDA/policy optimization), a genuinely underexplored angle relative to prior work focused on inaccurate oracles.

Solid theoretical development: the paper carefully derives DADO from classical message-passing for exact optimization, generalizes to distributional value functions with a clear lower-bound justification, and additionally provides an independent max-entropy/soft-Q derivation (Sec. A.4) that arrives at a structurally similar algorithm, lending credibility and generality to the approach.

Good positioning relative to related work, clearly distinguishing DADO from FDA, Bayesian-network EDAs (Pelikan), chain-structured RL policy optimization, and additive-model Bayesian optimization, explaining why none of these can handle general junction-tree-structured coordination via message-passing.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical validation: synthetic landscapes at multiple sequence lengths (up to L=200) with controlled reciprocal sign epistasis, plus real protein property predictors (4+3 datasets) built from AlphaFold3 structural contact graphs, showing consistent (though not universal) improvements over a naive EDA.

Useful ablations: sample-budget (K) sweeps and a case study varying the contact-distance threshold t that shows a clear, interpretable tradeoff between decomposition strength, predictive accuracy, and optimization speed (GB1 case).
Reproducibility is supported by detailed hyperparameter sweep description and public code release.
weaknesses: The primary empirical baseline throughout is only a decomposition-unaware ('naive') EDA; despite explicitly discussing FDA and Bayesian-network-based EDAs as closest related work, no direct empirical comparison to these decomposition-aware alternatives is provided, making it hard to isolate the specific benefit of the message-passing/value-function coordination mechanism versus simpler factorization schemes.

The method assumes the junction tree decomposition is given or can be reliably constructed a priori (e.g., via AlphaFold3 contact thresholding); the sensitivity of results to decomposition misspecification is only lightly explored (one threshold sweep on GB1), and the harder problem of learning/discovering decompositions from data is left entirely to future work despite being central to real-world applicability.

Mixed and inconsistently explained results: TDP-43 shows no significant benefit, and the explanation offered (many near-optimal local optima) is speculative and not empirically substantiated; the Gcn4 case (poor decomposition due to intrinsic disorder) is included but its implications for practical deployment of the method are not deeply analyzed.

Search distributions are limited to simple MLP-based autoregressive factors; no exploration of more expressive generative models (e.g., VAEs, diffusion) is conducted despite these being highlighted as a key motivating advantage of the distributional optimization framing.

Evaluation remains purely in silico with learned/synthetic surrogate objectives rather than any real-world or wet-lab validation, limiting evidence of practical impact for the motivating scientific design applications (protein engineering, circuit design, telescope design) mentioned in the introduction.

The paper explicitly scopes out entropy regularization, priors, and conditioning (features central to practical AI-guided design pipelines like CbAS), which somewhat limits the demonstrated relevance to realistic design workflows despite claims about extensibility.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and reasonably rigorous theoretical derivation of DADO, connecting it to classical message-passing optimization, EDA/weighted-MLE updates, and a second independent derivation via a maximum-entropy/RL (soft value function) framework — the convergence of two derivations to similar algorithms lends some theoretical credibility.

The core idea — using junction-tree-structured value functions (a generalization of advantage-weighted regression from chain MDPs to arbitrary trees) to coordinate updates of a factorized search distribution — is a sensible and moderately novel generalization of existing EDA/FDA and policy-optimization-on-chains approaches.

The related work section carefully situates the contribution relative to FDA, Bayesian-network EDAs, chain-structured RL policy optimization, and additive-model Bayesian optimization, clarifying what is genuinely new.

Experiments span both fully synthetic functions (with controllable epistasis/difficulty) and four real protein property datasets (plus three more in the appendix), together with ablations on sample budget K and on the contact-distance threshold controlling decomposition strength (GB1 case study), giving some breadth.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: full algorithmic pseudocode, hyperparameter sweep details, dataset descriptions, and a stated intent to release code.
weaknesses: Methodological circularity in the protein experiments: the "ground truth" oracle f(x) used for evaluation is itself an MLP explicitly constructed to respect the exact junction-tree decomposition that DADO is given as input. This guarantees the decomposition is exactly correct by construction, which is unrealistic (real predictive oracles, e.g., learned fitness models or wet-lab assays, are not exactly decomposable in this way) and likely inflates DADO's apparent advantage; the paper does not test robustness to decomposition misspecification relative to a truly independent oracle (e.g., an unconstrained neural network or experimental assay).

The only baseline is a decomposition-unaware vanilla EDA. No comparison is made to other decomposition-exploiting methods explicitly discussed in the paper (FDA, Bayesian-network EDAs, additive-model Bayesian optimization), nor to simpler decomposition-aware heuristics (e.g., independent per-factor optimization without message-passing, or classical exact message-passing as an oracle upper bound to quantify the optimality gap of DADO's distributional solutions).

Learning/estimating the decomposition itself — arguably the hardest and most practically important step for real applications — is not solved here; the method assumes a decomposition is given (from thresholded AlphaFold3 contacts) and estimating decomposability is explicitly deferred as "active area of research," limiting the practical applicability of the contribution beyond proof-of-concept.

Important extensions needed for realistic design settings (entropy regularization, conditioning on a pretrained unconditional generative model, accounting for oracle inaccuracy/uncertainty as in CbAS/CbAS-like methods) are explicitly excluded and left to future work, making the empirical demonstration feel preliminary relative to state-of-the-art AI-guided design pipelines.

No analysis of computational overhead (wall-clock time, memory, number of forward/backward passes) of DADO relative to the naive EDA, despite DADO requiring many more sub-networks, sequential conditional sampling, and tree-structured value function computation — a concern for real scalability claims.

Evaluation is limited to per-iteration sample-mean curves of f(x); no reporting of best-found design, sequence diversity, held-out validation beyond the predictive model's own accuracy, or any biologically grounded validation, limiting insight into practical design quality beyond mean optimization speed.

Hyperparameters (learning rate, shaping temperature β) are tuned separately per method and per function based on final-iteration performance, which, combined with relatively small-scale sweeps for protein experiments (54 combinations vs 100 for synthetic), raises some concern about fairness/stability of the comparison.

The scalability of the method to junction-tree nodes with more than one variable is acknowledged but not empirically explored for the protein experiments in a way that stresses the harder soft-decomposability regime (overlapping meta-variables with large cliques), and the dismissal of neural-network-based synthetic component functions as "overly smooth" is not rigorously justified.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated unification of classical junction-tree message-passing with distributional optimization (EDA/policy optimization), yielding a principled way to exploit known decomposability of a scientific objective for more sample-efficient search.

Two independent derivations of essentially the same algorithm (a lower-bound argument on value functions and a maximum-entropy/soft-Q derivation connecting to RL as inference) strengthen confidence in the soundness and generality of the approach.

Clear positioning relative to related work (FDA, Bayesian-network EDAs, chain-structured policy optimization in RL, additive-model Bayesian optimization), correctly identifying DADO as a generalization of chain-based coordination to arbitrary junction trees.

Reasonably thorough empirical evaluation: controlled synthetic functions with tunable decomposability/epistasis and sequence length, plus four (plus three appendix) real protein property datasets with structure-derived decompositions via AlphaFold3 contact maps.

Useful ablations examining the effect of sample budget K and the decomposition strictness (contact threshold t) on the relative advantage of DADO over a naive EDA, showing sensible trends (looser threshold/less decomposed hurts DADO's advantage, more samples help both).
Good reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameter sweeps, architecture choices, and a public code repository.
weaknesses: The only baseline compared throughout is a decomposition-unaware naive EDA; no empirical comparison to other decomposition-aware methods discussed in related work (FDA, Bayesian-network EDA, additive-model BO), despite these being natural competitors.

The method presupposes a known or algorithmically-derivable decomposition (via thresholded contact graphs); there is no treatment of decomposition misspecification robustness beyond a single case study (GB1 threshold sweep), nor joint learning of the decomposition, which is left entirely to future work.

Synthetic experiments are restricted to junction trees with singleton nodes (node size 1) because larger cliques would require intractable or unrealistically smooth tabular/NN component functions, limiting insight into how DADO behaves under richer, higher-cardinality decompositions typical of real design problems.

No real-world/wet-lab or external benchmark validation; all property functions are either synthetic or fit in-house to existing assay data, so claims of practical utility for actual protein design remain somewhat speculative.

The paper explicitly omits entropy regularization, priors, and conditioning (as in CbAS-style approaches) that are typically essential for realistic, uncertainty-aware design; the stripped-down EDA setting, while clarifying, reduces the immediate practical relevance of the demonstrated gains.
Mixed results (e.g., TDP-43 showing no significant improvement) are explained post hoc as a saturated/easy landscape without independent verification of this hypothesis.
Large number of statistical comparisons (many p-values across figures) without correction for multiple comparisons, somewhat weakening the strength of the significance claims.

strengths: Presents a well-motivated and technically rigorous generalization of Estimation-of-Distribution Algorithms (EDAs) to leverage known decomposability of the objective function via a junction-tree formulation, complete with a clean generalization of classical max-plus message passing to distributional value functions.

Provides multiple, complementary derivations of the method (direct message-passing derivation in the main text/Sec. A.4, and an independent maximum-entropy/probabilistic-graphical-model derivation in Sec. A.5), lending credibility and generality to the core algorithmic idea.

Extensive empirical evaluation: synthetic functions with controlled decomposition across varying sequence length (L up to 400) and alphabet size (D up to 100), plus four real protein property-prediction landscapes (AAV, Amyloid, Gcn4, TDP-43) derived from AlphaFold3 structures, with statistically significant improvements over baselines (paired t-tests, 20 seeds, confidence intervals).
Good set of baselines within the EDA family (naive EDA, FDA, PPO-style update) that isolate the contribution of factorized search distributions versus message-passing value functions.

Thorough robustness and ablation studies (Sec. A.9): effect of contact threshold on decomposability/accuracy trade-off, random graph mutation robustness, runtime comparisons, and behavior on less-decomposable proteins (GB1, ynzC, CreiLOV), which honestly reports cases where the method's advantage shrinks.
Detailed reproducibility documentation (architectures, hyperparameter sweeps, dataset sources, training details) in the appendix.
weaknesses: The method fundamentally depends on a known or inferable decomposition (junction tree); the only concrete mechanism shown for obtaining this in a real domain is an AlphaFold3-contact-thresholding heuristic for proteins, which is somewhat ad hoc and not validated in any other scientific design domain (circuits, materials, telescopes) mentioned as motivating examples.

Empirical comparisons are limited to baselines within the same EDA/policy-optimization lineage (naive EDA, FDA, PPO-style update); no comparison to other widely used generative/model-based design approaches referenced in related work (e.g., CbAS, autofocused oracles, Bayesian optimization with additive structure) that could contextualize DADO's benefit relative to the broader design literature.

On less-decomposable real proteins (GB1, ynzC, CreiLOV, relegated to the appendix) DADO's advantage over FDA and even the naive EDA diminishes or disappears, indicating the method's benefits are contingent on favorable decomposition structure that may not hold broadly, somewhat undercutting the generality of the main claims.

The paper explicitly sets aside the accuracy of the learned property predictor f(x) as out of scope, yet real-world utility of the discovered high-scoring designs depends critically on this accuracy; no wet-lab or independent-oracle validation is provided to confirm that optimized designs are truly higher quality rather than exploiting predictor artifacts.

The reproducibility section states code is available on GitHub but the actual repository link is missing/blank in the provided manuscript, undermining verification of the reproducibility claim as presented.

The exposition is dense and heavily notation-laden (multiple redundant derivations across main text and appendix), which may hinder accessibility for readers less familiar with message passing and EDA/RL formalisms.

strengths: Clean theoretical generalization of classical junction-tree message passing to distributional optimization (EDA/policy-optimization style), with two independent derivations (value-function lower bound and maximum-entropy/KL matching) that arrive at essentially the same update rule, lending credibility to the approach.

Comprehensive experimental program: synthetic functions at multiple sequence lengths (L=25,50,200,400) and alphabet sizes (D=20,50,100), plus four (and in the appendix, all seven) real protein property-predictor landscapes derived from AlphaFold3 contact maps, with 20-seed replication, paired t-tests, and confidence intervals.

Reasonable set of baselines (naive EDA, FDA which uses factorization without message-passing weighting, and a PPO-style update), which helps isolate the specific contribution of weighted message-passing coordination versus mere search-distribution factorization.

Thorough robustness/ablation analysis: sensitivity to the contact-threshold used to build the decomposition, random edge-mutation perturbation of the decomposition graph, and holdout predictive accuracy of decomposed vs. non-decomposed property models, showing the method is fairly tolerant to imperfect a priori decomposition knowledge.
Good reproducibility: detailed algorithm box, exhaustive hyperparameter and architecture description, dataset documentation, runtime comparison table, and a stated intent to release code.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to prior work: FDA (Mühlenbein & Mahnig, 1999) already factorizes the search distribution according to a decomposition; DADO's main addition is weighting updates via message-passing value functions, and the paper's own appendix results (GB1, ynzC, CreiLOV) show FDA performs comparably to or better than DADO when junction-tree nodes are large, undercutting the claimed general advantage of message-passing coordination.

All evaluation is performed in silico against neural-network property predictors fit to existing assay data (or synthetic functions), with no real experimental/wet-lab validation of designed sequences; because the search distribution is optimized against the same type of model used to construct the decomposition, there is a risk of reward hacking/overfitting to predictor artifacts that is not assessed.

The method's benefits are shown to depend heavily on the design problem admitting a sparse, low-max-clique decomposition (e.g., via AlphaFold3 contact thresholding); for proteins with less sparse structure (GB1, ynzC, CreiLOV) the advantage shrinks or disappears, raising concerns about applicability to many real-world problems with higher-order or diffuse epistasis, which the paper only partially investigates.

The construction of the decomposition itself (contact threshold, junction tree algorithm) is heuristic and somewhat ad hoc; while robustness experiments are included, they are limited to one protein (GB1) and small random edge perturbations, which may not reflect realistic model-misspecification scenarios in other domains such as circuits or materials that the paper claims as target applications.

No comparison to more standard model-based/Bayesian optimization baselines used in the protein design literature (e.g., CbAS, conditioning-by-adaptive-sampling, or GP-based additive BO methods), despite these being discussed in related work; the chosen baselines (naive EDA, FDA, PPO) are reasonable but somewhat narrow for substantiating broader significance.

The paper explicitly defers the realistic and important complication of predictor inaccuracy/out-of-distribution generalization to future work, which somewhat limits the demonstrated practical significance of the method for actual AI-driven scientific design, where predictive models are rarely accurate everywhere.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated theoretical contribution: DADO generalizes classical max-plus message passing on junction trees to the distributional optimization (EDA/policy-optimization) setting, providing a principled way to exploit known/assumed decomposability of the objective for more sample-efficient search.

Two independent derivations are given (a value-function lower-bound derivation in the main text/Sec. A.4, and an alternative maximum-entropy/RL-style derivation in Sec. A.5) that arrive at essentially the same algorithm, lending credibility and generality to the framework and connecting it to existing EDA, RL (advantage-weighted regression, PPO), and probabilistic graphical model literatures.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation: controlled synthetic experiments across increasing sequence length (L=25 to 400) and alphabet size (D=20,50,100) that cleanly show DADO's advantage grows with problem scale, plus real-world anchored experiments on four protein property predictors (AAV, Amyloid, Gcn4, TDP-43) derived from AlphaFold3 structures.

Thorough ablation/robustness studies in the appendix: sensitivity to the contact-threshold hyperparameter used to build the decomposition graph, robustness to random edge addition/removal in the decomposition graph, holdout predictive accuracy of decomposed vs. non-decomposed models, and runtime comparisons — these substantially strengthen the paper's claim that near-exact a priori knowledge of decomposability is not required.
Good transparency/reproducibility: detailed algorithm (Alg. 1), exhaustive hyperparameter sweep descriptions, dataset sourcing, and a stated commitment to release code.

Appropriate, though limited, baselines (naive EDA, FDA, PPO-style EDA) that isolate the specific contribution of value-function-weighted factorized updates versus merely factorizing the search distribution (FDA) or using PPO-style clipping.
weaknesses: Baselines are restricted to decomposition-aware/unaware EDA variants (EDA, FDA, PPO); no comparison to other modern model-based or generative design baselines commonly used in the sequence-design literature (e.g., CbAS, adaptive sampling with conservative/robust oracles, gradient-based discrete samplers), which limits positioning relative to the broader design literature even though the paper's primary claim is about exploiting decomposability rather than oracle robustness.

On several real protein datasets with less favorable decomposability (GB1, ynzC, CreiLOV, reported only in the appendix), DADO's advantage over baselines shrinks or becomes comparable to FDA, suggesting the method's practical benefit is contingent on the degree of decomposability present, which is not guaranteed in general scientific design problems.

The decomposition graph for proteins is obtained via a simple residue-distance threshold on AlphaFold3 structures — a coarse and somewhat ad hoc heuristic; no demonstration is given for constructing useful decompositions in other claimed application domains (circuits, materials, telescope design) mentioned as motivation.

All protein experiments optimize against in silico neural-network property predictors fit to existing assay data rather than against real wet-lab validation, so claims of "practical utility" are indirect; this is acknowledged as out of scope but still limits the practical significance of the empirical results.

Wall-clock runtime of DADO is not meaningfully better than the naive EDA (Table 1) despite its lower-dimensional sub-problems, which is a bit surprising and undercuts the narrative of DADO being more "efficient"; this is noted but not deeply analyzed.

The paper is dense and heavy on notation (multiple nested derivations, many symbols for value/Q-functions), which may hinder accessibility; more intuition/diagrams earlier could help a broader readership.

Statistical testing relies on paired t-tests comparing final-iteration means across 20 seeds for many separate comparisons without correction for multiple comparisons, which is a minor but persistent statistical rigor concern across the many reported p-values.
